summary: hiking time (How long your hike will take) is what the Hiking time calculator works out, and it gets there from the distance, the break time and the hiking time. It suits a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Hiking time calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hiking time calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports hiking time (How long your hike will take) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the ground conditions and the going downhill); then you type in the distance, the break time, the hiking time (How long your hike will take) and the hiking time (How long your hike will take).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hiking time calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Hiking time=(1 ÷ 600) × ascent + break time − 1 ÷ 1200 × descent + (1 ÷ 5) × distance
Hiking time=(1 ÷ 600) × ascent + break time − 1 ÷ 1200 × descent + (1 ÷ 4) × distance
Ascent=-600 × break time − 1 ÷ 2 × descent − 120 × distance + 600 × hiking time
Ascent=-600 × break time − 1 ÷ 2 × descent − 150 × distance + 600 × hiking time

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Ground conditions set to Paths, tracks, and roads, Going downhill set to Gentle decline (5°-12°), Distance = 30 km and Ascent = 30 m. The calculator returns Hiking time = 10 hrs.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Hiking time = 10 hrs should be roughly the size you expected from Ground conditions set to Paths, tracks, and roads and Going downhill set to Gentle decline (5°-12°).

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in kilometers

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hiking time calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the distance, the break time and the hiking time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Hiking time calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns hiking time (How long your hike will take), derived from the distance, the break time and the hiking time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hiking time calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance, the break time and the hiking time, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Hiking time = 10 hrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hiking time calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
